She is sent to the English countryside for safety where she encounters some drama that changes her life forever. Teachers, if you're looking for a fast-paced and easy-to-read mystery, be sure to pick up I Follow the Rules.

The poem was good, but the next day another man noted on Jonas' poem, "Write me a poem that requires no record to be kept of what cats did on a certain day or in a certain hour." Jonas sat in the cafe again and soon wrote "The Cat and The Silence." When fire swept the forest and levees failed and the days were hot and eerie and red, the cat that slept all day and woke at 4 A.M. didn't care. It watched the moon wane and birds fall from the sky, and waited for the world to end. The man who'd left the note on "The Cat and The Box" liked "The Cat and The Silence" even more. "Write me a poem about your favorite color," the note read one morning. "But you must not use the word blue or any of its shades," the note continued. The man who'd left the note sat alone in the front window of the cafe, reading the morning paper. His hair was white and his hands shook as he turned the paper's pages. "Write only of colors that are red or gray," the note read. "And do not speak of purple or the gold in autumn leaves or green Pasture or darker shades." Jonas was puzzled, but he soon began to write—not of blue, but of ozone, and gray, and the way the world was sometimes gold or green or red. The poem was good. "Now write one about 'blue.'"

The man who gave Jonas all of those assignments was a theoretical physicist. He wasn't insane. He would, however, have said that anyone who thought the world could be saved was. "Where do poems come from?" Jonas asked him later, when all the poems were done. "From the ether," the man said. "From the place that holds the world together and is stimulated by it." "When the world ends. . . ." Jonas began. "So will the ether," the man said.

What colors do leaves turn in autumn?
If you're like most people who live in the Northern Hemisphere, you're probably thinking of the bright reds, oranges, and even has of gold you usually see.
American ginkgo trees turn a buttery yellow and some sugar maples turn brilliant crimson, but others, such as oaks, elms, and beech trees, turn various shades of brown.
Why do some leaves turn one color, and other leaves another color?
The truth is one of nature's best kept secrets, and scientists still haven't been able to completely solve the mystery.
Some progress has been made, and part of the answer has to do with mitochon­dria, the tiny organelles in plant and animal cells that make energy. Scientists now know that autumn colors are in part due to chemicals in the cells of trees known as mito­chondrial death proteins.
Beginning in late summer, as the nights grow longer and there's less sun­light, a layer of cells known as the abscission layer forms between the stem of a leaf and its petiole.
Once the cells in the abscission layer are sealed off, the leaves no longer receive nutrients, and they start to change color and fall.
As the green chlorophyll disappears from the leaf, the other chemicals in the leaf begin to show their colors.
Some of the most vibrant colors are produced from anthocyanin pigments, which are stimulated to appear when there are lots of sunny days and cool nights, as well as from carotenoid pigments, such as xanthophyll, which are always present in the leaf.
The weather also plays a role in determining what colors we'll see each autumn.
A warm wet autumn will cause the production of the vivid red pigments in the leaf to stop early, and the leaves will turn brown and fall sooner.
A warm dry autumn will cause the production of the brilliant yellow pigments to stop early and, once again, the leaves will turn brown and fall early.

512.completion:
stood up. 
 As he walked out of the classroom, he saw a girl in the hallway who was crying. Her name was Charlotte, and she was the new student in the class. Jonas stopped and asked her if she was okay. She shook her head, and Jonas took her hand and led her to a spot on the hill across the street from their home. It was the special spot where the wind played, where they could watch the sun set.
 They sat there for a long time, and Jonas listened as Charlotte told him about her old school, how everyone made fun of her, and how she didn't have any friends. Jonas felt a hole open up in his chest as he listened to her, and he realized that he had never thought about what it might be like to be her.
 He had always assumed that everyone felt the same way he did, that everyone liked to read and play music. He had never considered that someone might feel lonely and out of place. This realization made Jonas uneasy, and he decided that he would try harder to be a good citizen, to follow the rules, and to fit in.
 The next day at school, Jonas made a conscious effort to blend in with the other students. He listened to the teacher carefully, took notes, and completed his assignments on time. He didn't raise his hand in class, and he didn't ask any questions. He simply did what was expected of him.
 After school, Jonas went to the cafeteria for dinner. He sat with a group of students who were talking and laughing, and he tried to join in on their conversation. They were discussing the latest fashions and the upcoming school dance. Jonas had no interest in either topic, but he forced himself to listen and chime in when he could.
 As he left the cafeteria, Jonas saw Charlotte sitting alone at a table. She looked up at him and smiled, and Jonas felt a pang of guilt. He had promised himself that he would try to be a good citizen, but he couldn't help feeling like he was betraying a part of himself by pretending to care about things he didn't.
 That evening, Jonas sat down at his desk and began to write. He wrote about the things he loved, about the joy he found in reading and playing music, about the way the wind sounded at the special spot on the hill. He wrote about Charlotte, and how she had taught him that there were other ways of being, other ways of feeling.
 When he finished, Jonas looked at the page and smiled.

Mira sat at her desk and began to work. Fall was her favorite time of year, but usually, she neglected to notice the leaves. Today, she paid close attention to their transformation.
Red, orange, deep yellow. The colors danced when the sun struck the leaves, just like the flames that danced in a fire. For the first time, Mira actually cared about the science behind the colors. Why did the leaves change? Why couldn't they stay green forever?
Mira's pencil flew across the paper as she wrote down facts that she'd learned in science class. She found pictures on her laptop and printed them out to illustrate her report. Then she added diagrams showing how the cells in leaves work.
As Mira worked, she had a chance to think about Olivia. At first, Olivia's comments had made her angry. But now Mira understood why Olivia had made them. Olivia was jealous because Mira's work was always neat and pretty. From now on, Mira would try to encourage her. "Maybe I can give her some tips," she thought.
*
Mira felt a tap on her shoulder. She turned to find Olivia standing behind her.
"Are you finished?" Olivia asked. She seemed nervous.
"Almost. Do you have any questions?" Mira asked. "I'd be happy to answer them."
Olivia handed Mira a card. "I wrote this down while you were working. Would you read it?"
Mira read Olivia's note. It said, "Your work is amazing. How do you make it look so good? What's your secret?"
Mira looked up. "It's not a secret. I'd be happy to share my tricks with you."
Mira spent the next few minutes showing Olivia how she outlined her ideas before she started writing, how she made sure her handwriting was clear, and how she highlighted important facts with pictures and diagrams.
Olivia smiled as she took notes. "Can we work together on out next science project?" she asked.
Mira grinned. "I'd love to!"
Since that day, Mira and Olivia have worked side by side in science class. Working together, their projects are even more amazing than their individual ones ever were!
